publish_jobs.theorem_title: Block execution, original-index incidences, and whole-program compilation
publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
This library defines the interfaces that connect finite combinatorial counts to executable programs. For a light-language statement $s$, state $\sigma$, and resource limits $L$, it defines the resulting block state, block cost, block safety, and the assertion that a safe block establishes a postcondition. It also supplies counting-loop syntax, expression-value assertions, array passes, and structural rules for sequencing, branches, assignments, and stores.

For nonnegative block parameters $h,J$, integer modulus $P$, balancing offset $d$, finite original-index sets, and integer-valued input maps $a,b,c$, the library retains both original indices and complete representation choices. Its raw mass is the cardinality of these incidences; left and right bucket sizes count indices with the required residue conditions, so equal input values retain their multiplicity. The operational exponent is the maximum of the twelve entries of the fixed cost ledger:
$$\rho=\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\operatorname{costLedger}(E,\kappa,H(\theta_0))\bigr).$$
For a finite procedure list $P_0$, entry procedure $p_0$, and decision flag $\delta$, whole-program compilation concatenates initialization, the outermost call and verdict, compiled procedure bodies, a return dispatcher, and startup code. The compiler-test specification records the selected successor address, a step bound, and preservation of all nonscratch cells.

These definitions preserve the finite counting data and precise execution costs used by the deterministic integer 3SUM runtime proof. They adapt the attributed light-language and word-RAM infrastructure from the pinned source project; the library itself does not assert a new runtime theorem.

/-!
# Derived rules: time that is not typed, blocks, counting loops

The rules of this file spare the typing of step counts.  Ends.next gives the first statement its
time and the rest of the program what is left; Ends.setThen, Ends.storeThen and Ends.iteThen do the
same for one assignment, store or branch, and Ends.setLast, Ends.storeLast and Ends.iteLast treat
the last statement of a program.  `Ends.pieceThen` and `Ends.pieceLast` are the two forms for a
piece of the program that has a lemma of its own.  In every rule the main premises come first, then
the side conditions, and last the comparison of times.  The comparison has the default proof
`light_time`, safety conditions have the default proof `light_side`.

A block is a statement without loops and calls.  s.Runs lim σ R says that the block s runs safely
from σ and ends in a state that satisfies R; Ends.block turns this into a fact about time, with the
cost computed. Ends.whileBlock is the rule for a loop whose body is a block.

Stmt.for i hi body is the loop "for i = 0, …, hi - 1 do body".  The rule Ends.for owns the counter:
the safety of the test and of the increment and the number of steps of the loop are settled here,
once. Ends.forMem is the common case in which the body changes no local variable, so that the
invariant speaks about the memory only.  The three parts of every loop rule are called start, round
and done.  A loop rule is told a bound b on the steps of a round; for a round that is a block with
a name, say xRound, this is xRound.blockCost.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Light
open _root_.Light


variable {lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits} {P : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Program} {d : ℕ}

/-! ## Blocks -/

instance Cond.decidableHolds (σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : (c : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond) → Decidable (c.Holds σ)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a.val σ < b.val σ))
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => inferInstanceAs (Decidable (a.val σ = b.val σ))

/-- The state after a block (σ itself for a loop or a call, which are not blocks). -/
@[simp] def Stmt.after : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set x e, σ => { σ with loc := Function.update σ.loc x (e.val σ) }
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.store a e, σ => { σ with mem := Function.update σ.mem (a.val σ).toNat (e.val σ) }
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq s t, σ => t.after (s.after σ)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s t, σ => if c.Holds σ then s.after σ else t.after σ
  | _, σ => σ

/-- A bound on the number of steps of a block: the longer side of each branch counts (0 for a loop
or a call). -/
@[simp] def Stmt.blockCost : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set _ e => e.cost + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.store a e => a.cost + e.cost + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq s t => s.blockCost + t.blockCost
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s t => c.cost + 1 + max s.blockCost t.blockCost
  | _ => 0

/-- The statement is a block, and its run from σ stays within the limits. -/
@[simp] def Stmt.BlockSafe (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip, _ => True
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set _ e, σ => e.Safe lim σ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.store a e, σ => a.Safe lim σ ∧ e.Safe lim σ ∧ lim.Addr (a.val σ)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq s t, σ => s.BlockSafe lim σ ∧ t.BlockSafe lim (s.after σ)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s t, σ =>
    c.Safe lim σ ∧ (c.Holds σ → s.BlockSafe lim σ) ∧ (¬ c.Holds σ → t.BlockSafe lim σ)
  | _, _ => False

/-- The block s, started in σ, stays within the limits and ends in a state that satisfies R. -/
abbrev Stmt.Runs (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt) (σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) (R : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop) : Prop :=
  s.BlockSafe lim σ ∧ R (s.after σ)

/-! ## Sequencing: what is left of the time goes to the rest of the program -/

/-- The first statement gets T₁ steps, the rest of the program what is left of T. -/
theorem Ends.next {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {s₁ s₂ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop} (T₁ : ℕ)
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₁ σ T₁ fun σ' => _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₂ σ' (T - T₁) Q)
    (hT : T₁ ≤ T := by (first
                       | ( simp only [Stmt.blockCost✝, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.cost, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost, _root_.List.map_cons, _root_.List.map_nil, _root_.List.sum_cons, _root_.List.sum_nil, ]
                           first
                           | omega
                           | (ring_nf; omega))
                       | omega
                       |
                         (simp [] <;>
                             first
                             | omega
                             | (ring_nf; omega)))) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s₂)) σ T Q :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends.seq T₁ (T - T₁) h (by omega)

/-- Brackets do not matter: a piece of several statements, followed by the rest of the program, is
run statement by statement. -/
theorem Ends.seqAssoc {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {s₁ s₂ s₃ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝¹ s₂ s₃))) σ T Q) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝¹ s₁ s₂) s₃)) σ T Q := by
  obtain ⟨σ', _, he, hc, hq⟩ := h
  cases he with
  | seq he₁ he₂₃ =>
    cases he₂₃ with
    | seq he₂ he₃ => exact ⟨σ', _, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.seq (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.seq he₁ he₂) he₃, by omega, hq⟩

/-- A `skip` before the rest of the program takes no step. -/
theorem Ends.skipThen {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop} (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T Q) :
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip s)) σ T Q :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends.seq 0 T (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends.skip h) (by omega)

/-- A `skip` may be put behind a statement. -/
theorem Ends.skipLast {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip)) σ T Q) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T Q := by
  obtain ⟨σ', _, he, hc, hq⟩ := h
  cases he with
  | seq he₁ he₂ =>
    cases he₂
    exact ⟨σ', _, he₁, by omega, hq⟩

/-- A program that is defined as a sequence may be treated as the sequence. -/
theorem Ends.seqSelf {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {s₁ s₂ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s₂)) σ T Q) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s₂)) σ T Q :=
  h

/-- A piece of the program about which `h` is known, followed by the rest of the program, which gets
the steps that are left. -/
theorem Ends.pieceThen {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T T₁ : ℕ} {s₁ s₂ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {R Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₁ σ T₁ R) (rest : ∀ σ', R σ' → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₂ σ' (T - T₁) Q)
    (hT : T₁ ≤ T := by (first
                       | ( simp only [Stmt.blockCost✝, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.cost, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost, _root_.List.map_cons, _root_.List.map_nil, _root_.List.sum_cons, _root_.List.sum_nil, ]
                           first
                           | omega
                           | (ring_nf; omega))
                       | omega
                       |
                         (simp [] <;>
                             first
                             | omega
                             | (ring_nf; omega)))) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s₂)) σ T Q :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends.next T₁ (h.mono le_rfl rest) hT

/-- A piece of the program about which `h` is known, at the end of the program. -/
theorem Ends.pieceLast {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T T₁ : ℕ} {s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {R Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T₁ R) (rest : ∀ σ', R σ' → Q σ') (hT : T₁ ≤ T := by (first
                                                                                                                   | ( simp only [Stmt.blockCost✝, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.cost, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost, _root_.List.map_cons, _root_.List.map_nil, _root_.List.sum_cons, _root_.List.sum_nil, ]
                                                                                                                       first
                                                                                                                       | omega
                                                                                                                       | (ring_nf; omega))
                                                                                                                   | omega
                                                                                                                   |
                                                                                                                     (simp [] <;>
                                                                                                                         first
                                                                                                                         | omega
                                                                                                                         | (ring_nf; omega)))) :
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T Q :=
  h.mono hT rest











/-- A branch, followed by the rest of the program: each side, with the rest of the program behind
it, gets the steps that the test leaves. -/
theorem Ends.iteThen {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {c : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond} {s₁ s₂ s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (h₁ : c.Holds σ → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s)) σ (T - (c.cost + 1)) Q)
    (h₂ : ¬ c.Holds σ → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₂ s)) σ (T - (c.cost + 1)) Q)
    (hs : c.Safe lim σ := by (( (try have := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Std.space_le (by assumption))
                               (try have := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Std.const_le (by assumption))
                               simp [_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits.Addr, _root_.abs_le, -_root_.abs_mul, ] <;> omega))) (hT : c.cost + 1 ≤ T := by (first
                                                                    | ( simp only [Stmt.blockCost✝, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.cost, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost, _root_.List.map_cons, _root_.List.map_nil, _root_.List.sum_cons, _root_.List.sum_nil, ]
                                                                        first
                                                                        | omega
                                                                        | (ring_nf; omega))
                                                                    | omega
                                                                    |
                                                                      (simp [] <;>
                                                                          first
                                                                          | omega
                                                                          | (ring_nf; omega)))) :
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s₁ s₂) s)) σ T Q := by
  by_cases hc : c.Holds σ
  · obtain ⟨σ'', _, he, hk, hq⟩ := h₁ hc
    cases he with
    | seq he₁ he₂ => exact ⟨σ'', _, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.seq (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.iteTrue hs hc he₁) he₂, by omega, hq⟩
  · obtain ⟨σ'', _, he, hk, hq⟩ := h₂ hc
    cases he with
    | seq he₁ he₂ => exact ⟨σ'', _, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.seq (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.iteFalse hs hc he₁) he₂, by omega, hq⟩

/-- A branch, followed by the rest of the program, where the test says `p`: the first side is run
under the hypothesis `p`, the second under `¬ p`. -/
theorem Ends.iteIffThen {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {T : ℕ} {c : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond} {s₁ s₂ s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop}
    (p : Prop) (h₁ : p → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₁ s)) σ (T - (c.cost + 1)) Q)
    (h₂ : ¬ p → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ s₂ s)) σ (T - (c.cost + 1)) Q)
    (hs : c.Safe lim σ ∧ (c.Holds σ ↔ p) := by (( (try have := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Std.space_le (by assumption))
                                                 (try have := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Std.const_le (by assumption))
                                                 simp [_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits.Addr, _root_.abs_le, -_root_.abs_mul, ] <;> omega)))
    (hT : c.cost + 1 ≤ T := by (first
                               | ( simp only [Stmt.blockCost✝, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.cost, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost, _root_.List.map_cons, _root_.List.map_nil, _root_.List.sum_cons, _root_.List.sum_nil, ]
                                   first
                                   | omega
                                   | (ring_nf; omega))
                               | omega
                               |
                                 (simp [] <;>
                                     first
                                     | omega
                                     | (ring_nf; omega)))) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d ((_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq✝ (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s₁ s₂) s)) σ T Q :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends.iteThen (fun hc => h₁ (hs.2.1 hc)) (fun hc => h₂ fun hp => hc (hs.2.2 hp)) hs.1 hT

/-! ## Counting loops -/

/-!
# The compiler is correct on tests

The code of a test goes on to the next position if the test holds and jumps to a given position if
it does not, in at most as many steps as it has instructions, and it changes scratch cells only.
This behaviour is called `Decides`, and `decides_compileCond` proves it.

Both tests first evaluate a into T₀ and b into T₁ (`steps_pair`, which also serves the statement
that stores into the memory).  For a < b the code forms D = b - a - 1 and leaves if D < 0
(`decides_lt`).  For a = b it forms D = a - b and leaves if D < 0, then forms -D and leaves if that

one more (`inRange_sub`).

/-!
# The code of a whole program

`compileProgram P p0 dec` is the program of the word RAM that runs procedure p0 of the light
program P.  With dec = false it accepts at the end of the run; with dec = true it accepts if the
result of the procedure is positive and rejects if not.  It has five parts:

| position | part |
|---|---|
| 0 | `headCode`: the numbers 1, 0, -1, and a jump to the start-up code |
| `mainPos` | `mainCode`: the outermost statement `mainStmt p0`, then the verdict (`tailCode`) |
| `firstBody` | `bodiesCode`: the bodies of the procedures, each with its return sequence |
| `dispPos` | the dispatcher for the positions below `dispPos` |
| `3 * dispPos` | `startCode`: the pool, the outermost frame, and a jump back to `mainPos` |

The start-up code comes last so that no position in the rest of the code depends on its length.

The number `frameSize` of local variables of every frame is read off the text of P: it is the width
of the text.  The pool holds the numbers up to `dispPos`: every position to return to, and with them
the smaller numbers that the code needs (`two_mul_frameSize_add_le_dispPos`).

The facts proved here are about positions only: each part is where the table says
(`codeAt_headCode`, …, `codeAt_startCode`), and every body is at its entry (`codeAt_bodies`).
-/

# Local variables as a list

In the proof of a procedure body the state is written out as ⟨frame [a, b, …], μ⟩: the list
holds the local variables 0, 1, …, and all further ones are 0.  An assignment to local x replaces
entry x of the list (setLocal).  The rules of this file treat one statement each.  They are told the
value that is assigned or stored, and they ask for one fact about each expression: that its
evaluation stays within the limits and gives this value (Expr.Gives).  This fact and the comparison
of the costs are proved by default from the hypotheses in the context.  Ends.forFrame and
Ends.forShape are the rules for counting loops in this form.  In the names of the rules, To says
that the state is ⟨frame l, μ⟩.

Locals by name, and locals whose values do not matter:

* `setLocals l [(x, a), (y, b), …]` is the list `l` after the assignments `x := a`, `y := b`, ….
  With the names of the locals for `x`, `y`, … it describes the locals of a procedure by name:
  `setLocals [] [(Size, n), (Bound, U), …]`.
* `updateLocals loc [(x, a), (y, b), …]` is the same for locals that are not given as a list.  A
  lemma about a piece of text that several procedures share is stated for arbitrary locals `loc`.
* `refreshLocals l loc xs` is the list `l` with the entries `xs` read from `loc`.
* `LocalsBut xs l loc` says that `loc` agrees with `frame l` except perhaps at the locals `xs`.  In
  an invariant, `xs` are the scratch variables.  `Ends.asFrame` goes from such locals to a list, and
  `LocalsBut.of_eq` comes back.
* `Ends.pieceTo` and `Ends.pieceToThen` use a lemma about a piece of text that assigns only the
  locals `xs`: afterwards the locals are `refreshLocals l loc' xs`, where `loc'` are the locals of
  which the lemma speaks.  The lemma need not mention the locals that the piece does not assign.
* `Ends.forScratch` is the rule for a counting loop whose body may change the scratch variables
  `xs`: the round says nothing about the locals.
-/

publish_jobs.theorem_title: Global radix encoding, exact cost parameters, and compiler memory relations
publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
This bundle defines the concrete global encoding and the memory invariants used by the compiled deterministic integer 3SUM algorithm. For a local scale $h\in\mathbb N$, a retained choice records both an occurrence of a hash map in the deterministic local schedule and a disjoint-subset edge whose two hash buckets satisfy the prescribed cap. Keeping the occurrence preserves multiplicity even when maps repeat. Raw hashes sum canonical integer representatives before reduction modulo the selected prime $p_h$. For a depth $J\in\mathbb N$, the global modulus and representation cap are
$$M_{h,J}=p_h^J,\qquad R_{h,J}=(s_h b_h^2)^J,$$
where $s_h$ is the schedule length and $b_h$ is the local bucket cap. Output records retain the map occurrence and the union of the endpoint subsets; their global keys are positional radix hashes of the resulting integer contributions.

The analytic interface fixes the expansion-$232$ entropy quantities, the rational quartic switching function, and the exact rational constants $\varepsilon$, band shift, box saving, initial threshold, terminal fraction, and entropy ratio. Its twelve-entry cost ledger keeps each operational exponent separately. The bundle also includes the executable scale limits: if $u_m$, $s_m$, $a_m$, and $D_m$ denote the microblock size, total size, band exponent, and band divisor, respectively, then
$$\frac{u_m^2}{m}\to0,\quad \frac{s_m}{m}\to\varepsilon,\quad \frac{a_m}{m}\to(-\beta)\varepsilon,\quad \frac{\log D_m}{m}\to(\log2)(-\beta)\varepsilon$$
as the natural input scale $m$ tends to infinity, with $\beta$ the fixed band-shift parameter.

For word size $W\in\mathbb N$, the compiler's size data package its code layout, execution limits, stack capacity, and explicit word-fit inequalities. The relation between a Light state and a word-RAM memory specifies the constant cells, number pool, frame pointer, local-variable cells, and simulated nonnegative memory cells. A framed relation additionally requires the current frame to lie inside the stack. The writable-region predicate and arithmetic descriptions of temporary, stack, and pool cells support preservation under writes. Finally, a segment predicate states that a finite integer list occupies consecutive memory cells; its natural-number version uses integer casts.

These definitions connect finite radix representations and the exact analytic ledger to the concrete memory layout needed for compiler simulation and the complete runtime proof.

/-!
# The cells of the compiled code, and the memories that represent a state

The memory of the machine is one array indexed by the integers, and the compiled code keeps its
registers, temporaries, pool, stack and the memory of the light language in different parts of it.
Every proof about compiled code has to know that a write to one cell leaves the others alone.  This
file settles that once.

* Sets of cells: `Temps k F` (what evaluating an expression into T_k may change), `Scratch F` (what
  any compiled code uses freely), `Constants N` (what no compiled statement changes), `Writable Z q`
  (what a statement that runs in the frame q may change), and two parts of the memory, `Stack q Q`
  and `Pool N`.  "The memories m and m' differ only inside s" is `AgreeOutside s m m'`.
* The tactic `cells` proves that two cells are different, that a cell is or is not in one of these
  sets, or that one of these sets lies in another.  The tactic `cell_read` reads a cell of a memory
  that is given by writes.
* `Sizes W` collects the numbers that never change, with the assumptions on them: the layout of the
  code, the limits, the number of stack cells, and a word size W that fits them (`Fits`).
* `Rel Z σ q m`: the memory m represents the state σ in the frame q.  The relation survives changes
  of scratch cells (`Rel.same`) and of the stack beyond the frame (`Rel.beyond`); a write to the
  cell of a local variable or to a memory cell is the same write in the state (`Rel.setLoc`,
  `Rel.setMem`).  All four come from `Rel.of_agreeOutside`.  `Framed` adds that the frame lies
  within the stack.
* Two pieces of code that occur everywhere: the jump (`steps_jump`) and the two instructions that
  store a cell in a local variable (`steps_setVar`).

**Letters**, in this file and in the files on expressions, tests, calls and the simulation.
Numbers: W is the word size, F the number of local variables of a frame, N the largest number in the
pool, Q the number of stack cells, q a frame, pos a position in the code.  The temporaries are
written T₀, T₁, …, T_j; there are 2 F + 1 of them.
Facts: m, m₁, m₂, … are memories in the order in which they arise.  Z is a `Sizes`.  R says that a
memory represents a state (`Rel`), I the same with the frame inside the stack (`Framed`).  A says
that two memories agree outside a set of cells (`AgreeOutside`); A₂ speaks of m₂.  run is a run of
the machine (`Steps`).  val, va, vb say which number a cell holds.  hcode and names that end in Code
say where a piece of code is (`CodeAt`).
-/

@[expose] public section

open _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam
open _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam

namespace Light.Compiler
open _root_.Light.Compiler


open _root_.EndStatement renaming Instr -> Instr

/-! ## The numbers that never change -/

/-- The word size is large enough for the limits: words hold 2 · word + 2 (so the difference of two
values, and one less, is in range), all addresses of the memory, all addresses of a stack of Q
cells, and all numbers 0, …, N of the pool. -/
structure Fits (W : ℕ) (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (N Q : ℕ) : Prop where
  word : 2 * (2 * lim.word + 2) < (2 : ℤ) ^ W
  space : 2 * (lim.space : ℤ) < (2 : ℤ) ^ W
  stack : 2 * (2 * (Q : ℤ)) < (2 : ℤ) ^ W
  pool_lt : 2 * (N : ℤ) < (2 : ℤ) ^ W



/-- The numbers on which the proofs about compiled code depend: the layout of the code, the limits
on the runs of the light program, and the number of stack cells.  The pool holds the numbers from 0
to the position of the dispatcher. -/
structure Sizes (W : ℕ) extends _root_.Light.Compiler.CodeLayout where
  /-- The limits on the runs of the light program. -/
  lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits
  /-- The number of stack cells. -/
  Q : ℕ
  /-- The word size fits the limits, the pool and the stack. -/
  fits : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Fits W lim disp Q
  /-- The pool holds the numbers up to 2 (F + 1), which are the offsets in a frame. -/
  offsets_le : 2 * (F + 1) ≤ disp

/-! ## Sets of cells -/













/-- What the code of a statement that runs in the frame q may change: scratch cells, FP, the stack
cells from q on, and the memory cells within the limits. -/
def Writable {W : ℕ} (Z : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Sizes W) (q : ℕ) : Set ℤ :=
  _root_.Light.Compiler.Scratch Z.F ∪ {_root_.Light.Compiler.cFP} ∪ _root_.Light.Compiler.Stack q Z.Q ∪ {a | 0 ≤ a ∧ a < Z.lim.space}

/-! The temporaries, the stack and the pool are arithmetic progressions of cells. -/

theorem mem_temps_iff {k F : ℕ} {a : ℤ} :
    a ∈ _root_.Light.Compiler.Temps k F ↔ a = _root_.Light.Compiler.cADDR ∨ _root_.Light.Compiler.cT (2 * F) ≤ a ∧ a ≤ _root_.Light.Compiler.cT k ∧ 4 ∣ _root_.Light.Compiler.cT 0 - a := by
  simp only [_root_.Light.Compiler.Temps, _root_.Light.Compiler.cT, Set.mem_ofPred_eq]
  refine or_congr_right ⟨?_, fun h => ⟨((-23 - a) / 4).toNat, ?_⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨j, hk, hj, rfl⟩
    omega
  · omega

theorem mem_stack_iff {q Q : ℕ} {a : ℤ} :
    a ∈ _root_.Light.Compiler.Stack q Q ↔ _root_.Light.Compiler.cStack Q < a ∧ a ≤ _root_.Light.Compiler.cStack q ∧ 2 ∣ a := by
  simp only [_root_.Light.Compiler.Stack, _root_.Light.Compiler.cStack, Set.mem_ofPred_eq]
  refine ⟨?_, fun h => ⟨(-a / 2).toNat, ?_⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨j, hq, hj, rfl⟩
    omega
  · omega

theorem mem_pool_iff {N : ℕ} {a : ℤ} :
    a ∈ _root_.Light.Compiler.Pool N ↔ _root_.Light.Compiler.cPool N ≤ a ∧ a ≤ _root_.Light.Compiler.cPool 0 ∧ 4 ∣ _root_.Light.Compiler.cPool 0 - a := by
  simp only [_root_.Light.Compiler.Pool, _root_.Light.Compiler.cPool, Set.mem_ofPred_eq]
  refine ⟨?_, fun h => ⟨((-25 - a) / 4).toNat, ?_⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨n, hn, rfl⟩
    omega
  · omega







variable {W : ℕ} {Z : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Sizes W} {F : ℕ}











/-! ## Addresses, and numbers that fit in a word -/













/-! ## The relation between a state of the light language and a memory of the machine -/

/-- The memory m of the machine represents the state σ of a procedure whose frame is at q. -/
structure Rel (Z : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Sizes W) (σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) (q : ℕ) (m : ℤ → BitVec W) : Prop where
  one : m _root_.Light.Compiler.cONE = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W 1
  zero : m _root_.Light.Compiler.cZERO = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W 0
  neg : m _root_.Light.Compiler.cNEG = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W (-1)
  pool : ∀ n ≤ Z.disp, m (_root_.Light.Compiler.cPool n) = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W n
  fp : m _root_.Light.Compiler.cFP = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W (_root_.Light.Compiler.cStack q)
  loc : ∀ x < Z.F, m (_root_.Light.Compiler.cStack (q + x)) = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W (σ.loc x)
  mem : ∀ a < Z.lim.space, m (a : ℤ) = _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.wd W (σ.mem a)

section Rel

variable {σ σ' : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {q q' : ℕ} {m m' : ℤ → BitVec W}















end Rel

/-- The memory m represents the state σ in the frame q, and the frame lies within the stack: after
stack cell 0 and before stack cell Q. -/
structure Framed (Z : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Sizes W) (σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) (q : ℕ) (m : ℤ → BitVec W) : Prop where
  rel : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.Rel Z σ q m
  low : 1 ≤ q
  high : q + Z.F ≤ Z.Q

section code

variable {σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State} {q pos : ℕ} {m m' : ℤ → BitVec W} {code rest : List _root_.EndStatement.Instr}







end code

publish_jobs.theorem_title: Exact parameter bounds, local schedules, and the Light compiler interface
publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
This bundle joins the exact expansion-$232$ parameter interface to the semantics and compiler of the Light intermediate language. It includes certified rational intervals for the encoding quantities $E(232)$ and $\kappa(232)$, and the integer rounding facts for the executable schedule. For an input scale $m\in\mathbb N$, the microblock size is even, the block count is divisible by $20$, the total size has a nonnegative rounding deficit smaller than $20$ microblocks whenever the microblock size is positive, and the band divisor is positive.

For $h\in\mathbb N$, let $p_h$ be the selected local prime. The local field is $\mathbb Z/p_h\mathbb Z$; the deterministic schedule enumerates one-hot weight assignments on $464h$ coordinates and has length
$$320(2h+1)\bigl(\lfloor\log_2(p_h^2)\rfloor+1\bigr).$$

The compiler definitions give code and exact code-size functions for expressions, conditions, calls, and statements. Their width functions bound local-variable indices, call arities, and temporary requirements. For limits $\ell$, program $P$, call depth $d$, statement $s$, initial state $\sigma$, time allowance $T$, and postcondition $Q$, the predicate $\operatorname{Ends}(\ell,P,d,s,\sigma,T,Q)$ means that an execution ends in a state satisfying $Q$ with cost at most $T$. The bundle supplies basic compositional rules and the standard assumptions that addresses and program constants fit within the word bound.

For a problem $Q$ and real-valued time function $T(n,U)$, the word-RAM realization interface quantifies over every polynomial input bound $U=n^k$, including size zero, and allows a nonnegative constant-factor bound $c\max(T(n,U),0)+c$. The natural-valued step-bound conversion is
$$B_{C,a}(n)=\left\lceil C(n^a+1)\right\rceil_+\qquad(C,a\in\mathbb R,\ n\in\mathbb N).$$

These interfaces connect the exact rational parameter certificate, finite local schedules, operational Light proofs, and the final deterministic integer 3SUM runtime statement. They retain the pinned source project's compiler and machine conventions.

/-!
# The compiler from the light language to the word RAM: cells, and the code of statements

This file holds the definitions: the cells, the code of expressions, tests, statements, calls and
returns, the length of each piece of code, and the one condition on the text of a program (its
width).  The code of a whole program, `compileProgram`, puts these pieces together.

**Cells.**  A memory cell a of the light language is the cell a ≥ 0 of the machine.  Everything else
lives in negative cells.  A whole program takes two arguments from the cells -1 and -2 (`cARG1`,
`cARG2`) and puts its result into the cell -3 (`cRESULT`); the cell -4 is not used.  Odd cells from
-5 down hold the registers of the compiled code, the temporaries T₀, T₁, … for the evaluation of
expressions, and a pool of numbers: the cell `cPool n` holds the number n, for all n up to the
largest position to return to.  Even cells hold the call stack: stack cell j is the cell -2 j
(`cStack`).  The outermost frame of a whole program begins at stack cell `mainFrame` = 4, so the
code of its statements writes no stack cell before the cell -8 and leaves the cells -1, …, -4
alone.  The lemmas about pieces of code ask less: only that a frame begins after stack cell 0.

**Numbers.**  The constants of the program text are built from their binary digits where they are
needed.  The numbers that the compiled code itself needs, offsets in a frame and positions to return
to, come from the pool: the length of the code that builds a number from its digits depends on the
number, and a position to return to depends on the lengths.

**Frames.**  With F local variables per procedure, the frame of a running procedure is given by a
number q: local variable x is the cell -2 (q + x), the position to return to is in the
cell -2 (q - 1), and the register FP holds -2 q.  A call moves q to q + F + 1.

**Jumps.**  The machine only has "branch if negative" to a fixed position.  An unconditional jump
tests a register that holds -1.  A return loads the position r to return to into the register RR and
jumps to the dispatcher, the code "RR := RR - 1; if RR < 0 go to j" for j = 0, 1, 2, …, which
arrives at position r after 2 (r + 1) steps: a constant for a fixed program.

**Calls.**  The caller evaluates the arguments into temporaries, computes the address of the new
frame, fills its local variables (arguments first, then zeros), stores the position to return to,
moves FP and jumps to the procedure.  The procedure ends with its return sequence: result into RET,
position into RR, FP back to the caller's frame, jump to the dispatcher.  Back in the caller, RET is
stored into the variable that receives the result.

**Lengths.**  A jump forward needs the length of code that is not yet written, so the lengths are
defined on the text (`Expr.size`, `Cond.size`, `Stmt.size`) and then shown to be the lengths of the
code (`length_compileExpr`, `length_compileCond`, `length_compileStmt`).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Light.Compiler
open _root_.Light.Compiler


open _root_.EndStatement renaming Instr -> Instr

/-! ## Cells

The names of the registers are written in capitals, as in the comments on the code. -/


















/-! ## Expressions and tests -/







/-- Code that leaves the value of the expression in the temporary T_k, using only T_k, T_{k+1}, …
and ADDR.  A constant is built from its binary digits, in at most 2 log₂ n + 3 instructions. -/
def compileExpr : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℕ → List _root_.EndStatement.Instr
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const n, k => _root_.Light.Compiler.digitsCode (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k) (Nat.digits 2 n)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var x, k => [_root_.EndStatement.Instr.sub _root_.Light.Compiler.cADDR _root_.Light.Compiler.cFP (_root_.Light.Compiler.cPool (2 * x)), _root_.EndStatement.Instr.load (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k) _root_.Light.Compiler.cADDR]
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op o a b, k => compileExpr a k ++ compileExpr b (k + 1) ++ [o.instr (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k) (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k) (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT (k + 1))]
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a, k => compileExpr a k ++ [_root_.EndStatement.Instr.load (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k) (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT k)]

/-- The length of the code of an expression. -/
def _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.size : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const n => _root_.Light.Compiler.digitsLen (Nat.digits 2 n)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var _ => 2
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op _ a b => a.size + b.size + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.size + 1

/-- Code that goes on to the next position if the test holds and jumps to the position l if it does
not.  Both tests evaluate a into T₀ and b into T₁.  For a < b the code forms D = b - a - 1 and
leaves if D < 0.  For a = b it forms D = a - b and leaves if D < 0, then forms -D and leaves if that
is negative. -/
def compileCond : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond → ℕ → List _root_.EndStatement.Instr
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b, l =>
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.compileExpr a 0 ++ _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.compileExpr b 1 ++ [_root_.EndStatement.Instr.sub _root_.Light.Compiler.cD (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT 1) (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT 0), _root_.EndStatement.Instr.sub _root_.Light.Compiler.cD _root_.Light.Compiler.cD _root_.Light.Compiler.cONE, _root_.EndStatement.Instr.bltz _root_.Light.Compiler.cD l]
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b, l =>
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.compileExpr a 0 ++ _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.compileExpr b 1 ++
      [_root_.EndStatement.Instr.sub _root_.Light.Compiler.cD (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT 0) (_root_.Light.Compiler.cT 1), _root_.EndStatement.Instr.bltz _root_.Light.Compiler.cD l, _root_.EndStatement.Instr.sub _root_.Light.Compiler.cD _root_.Light.Compiler.cZERO _root_.Light.Compiler.cD, _root_.EndStatement.Instr.bltz _root_.Light.Compiler.cD l]

/-- The length of the code of a test. -/
def _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.size : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => a.size + b.size + 3
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => a.size + b.size + 4

/-! ## Statements -/



/-- The arguments of a call, evaluated into T_k, T_{k+1}, …. -/
def argsCode : List _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℕ → List _root_.EndStatement.Instr
  | [], _ => []
  | e :: es, k => _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Compiler.compileExpr e k ++ argsCode es (k + 1)

/-- The length of the code for the arguments of a call. -/
def argsSize : List _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℕ
  | [] => 0
  | e :: es => e.size + argsSize es





/-- A call up to and including the jump to the procedure; ret is the position after the jump. -/

/-! ## The width of a text

The compiled code gives every frame the same number F of local variables.  That is enough if F is at
least the width of every body: a number that bounds the variables, the arguments of each call, and
the temporaries that each expression needs.  Then 2 F + 1 temporaries are enough too: up to F
arguments of a call wait in temporaries while the last one is evaluated in up to F more.  "The width
is at most F" is taken apart by one lemma for each construct. -/

/-- One more than the largest variable of an expression. -/

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const _ => 0
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var x => x + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op _ a b => max a.vars b.vars
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.vars

/-- The number of temporaries that the code of an expression uses. -/

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const _ => 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var _ => 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op _ a b => max a.height (b.height + 1)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.height

/-- The width of an expression: at least its variables and its temporaries. -/
def Expr.width (e : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr) : ℕ := max e.vars e.height

/-- The width of a test: that of its two sides. -/

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => max a.width b.width
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => max a.width b.width



/-- The width of a statement: at least the width of its expressions, one more than each variable
that it writes, and the number of arguments of each of its calls. -/
def Stmt.width : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip => 0
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set x e => max (x + 1) e.width
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.store a e => max a.width e.width
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq s t => max s.width t.width

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.while c s => max c.width s.width

/-!
# Proof rules for the light language

Ends lim P d s σ T Q says: the statement s, started in σ, ends within T steps in a state that
satisfies Q.  There is one rule for each construct; a rule turns a goal about a statement into goals
about its parts, so a proof follows the text of the program from top to bottom.  Recursion needs no
rule: a statement about a recursive procedure is proved by induction (in Lean) on a measure, and the
rule for calls unfolds the body.

There are three rules for loops: with an invariant indexed by the number of the round and a cost for
each round (Ends.while), the same with one cost for all rounds (Ends.whileConst), and, for a loop
whose number of rounds depends on the data, with a quantity that every round decreases
(Ends.whileVariant).

The file also has the basic facts about runs (a run stays a run when procedures are appended to the
program), notation for writing programs, the simplification set
`light_norm`, and the standing assumptions `Std` about the limits.
-/

@[expose] public section

open _root_.Light


variable {lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits} {P : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Program} {d : ℕ}

/-! ## Runs -/





/-- Procedure number i of a list that is appended to the program P₀ has the number |P₀| + i. -/
theorem getElem?_append_length_add (P₀ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Program) {R : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Program} {i : ℕ} {body : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt}
    (h : R[i]? = some body) : (P₀ ++ R)[P₀.length + i]? = some body := by
  rw [List.getElem?_append_right (by omega), Nat.add_sub_cancel_left]
  exact h

/-- The statement s, started in σ, ends within T steps in a state that satisfies Q. -/

    Prop :=
  ∃ σ' c, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec lim P d s σ σ' c ∧ c ≤ T ∧ Q σ'

/-- More time and a weaker conclusion. -/
theorem Ends.mono {s σ T T' Q Q'} (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T Q) (hT : T ≤ T')
    (hQ : ∀ σ', Q σ' → Q' σ') : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s σ T' Q' := by
  obtain ⟨σ', c, he, hc, hq⟩ := h
  exact ⟨σ', c, he, hc.trans hT, hQ _ hq⟩



theorem Ends.skip {σ T} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop} (h : Q σ) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip σ T Q :=
  ⟨σ, 0, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.skip, Nat.zero_le _, h⟩

theorem Ends.set {σ T x e} {Q : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → Prop} (hs : e.Safe lim σ) (hT : e.cost + 1 ≤ T)
    (h : Q { σ with loc := Function.update σ.loc x (e.val σ) }) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set x e) σ T Q :=
  ⟨_, _, _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Exec.set hs, hT, h⟩

    (h : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₁ σ T₁ fun σ' => _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Ends lim P d s₂ σ' T₂ Q) (hT : T₁ + T₂ ≤ T) :

      fun σ' => Q ⟨Function.update σ.loc x (σ'.loc 0), σ'.mem⟩)

  obtain ⟨σ', k, he, hk, hq⟩ := h

Not trusted: a theorem about a program does not depend on how the program was typed in. -/

/-!
# A running time that is realized on the word RAM

The deductions between running-time claims are made for an arbitrary reading `M : DetTimeModel` of
"is solved by a deterministic algorithm in time T".  `RealizedWithin` is the link to programs: the
problem is solved on the word RAM, in its input layout, within `c T + c` steps.
-/

@[expose] public section

open _root_.EndStatement renaming Instr -> Instr

namespace ThreeSumApsp.WordRam
open _root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam




/-- `RealizedWithin` for a problem of the form of `EndStatement.lean`, on the instances of all
sizes, 0 included: for every exponent `κ` some program solves all instances whose numbers are
bounded by `U = n^κ`, within `c max(T, 0) + c` steps. (A running time `T n U` says nothing at
`n = 0`.) -/
def Realized (Q : _root_.EndStatement.Problem) (T : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ κ : ℕ, ∃ (P : List _root_.EndStatement.Instr) (b : ℕ) (c : ℝ), 0 ≤ c ∧
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.Solves (_root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.ofEnd Q) P b (fun x => x.U = x.n ^ κ) (fun x => c * max (T x.n x.U) 0 + c)

end ThreeSumApsp.WordRam

end

end ThreeSum1960614.Machine

/-!
# From a real exponent to a rational one

An item statement bounds the steps of a program by `C (n^a + 1)`, with real numbers `C` and `a`.
The end statement uses Lean's core library only.  It asks for a step bound `T` with natural values
that depends on the size alone, and it writes `T(n) = O(n^r)`, for a rational `r = p/q`, as
`T(n)^q ≤ K n^p`.  Here the first bound, rounded up, is shown to be a bound of the second kind
(`bigO_stepBound`), and a program that meets the first is shown to meet the second
(`SolvedInTime.endStatement`).  The program and the slope of the word size stay the same.
-/

public section

/-- The bound `C (n^a + 1)` of `SolvedInTimeAt` for `e = 0`, rounded up. -/

publish_jobs.theorem_title: Exact parameter bounds, local schedules, and the Light compiler interface
publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
This bundle joins the exact expansion-$232$ parameter interface to the semantics and compiler of the Light intermediate language. It includes certified rational intervals for the encoding quantities $E(232)$ and $\kappa(232)$, and the integer rounding facts for the executable schedule. For an input scale $m\in\mathbb N$, the microblock size is even, the block count is divisible by $20$, the total size has a nonnegative rounding deficit smaller than $20$ microblocks whenever the microblock size is positive, and the band divisor is positive.

For $h\in\mathbb N$, let $p_h$ be the selected local prime. The local field is $\mathbb Z/p_h\mathbb Z$; the deterministic schedule enumerates one-hot weight assignments on $464h$ coordinates and has length
$$320(2h+1)\bigl(\lfloor\log_2(p_h^2)\rfloor+1\bigr).$$

The compiler definitions give code and exact code-size functions for expressions, conditions, calls, and statements. Their width functions bound local-variable indices, call arities, and temporary requirements. For limits $\ell$, program $P$, call depth $d$, statement $s$, initial state $\sigma$, time allowance $T$, and postcondition $Q$, the predicate $\operatorname{Ends}(\ell,P,d,s,\sigma,T,Q)$ means that an execution ends in a state satisfying $Q$ with cost at most $T$. The bundle supplies basic compositional rules and the standard assumptions that addresses and program constants fit within the word bound.

For a problem $Q$ and real-valued time function $T(n,U)$, the word-RAM realization interface quantifies over every polynomial input bound $U=n^k$, including size zero, and allows a nonnegative constant-factor bound $c\max(T(n,U),0)+c$. The natural-valued step-bound conversion is
$$B_{C,a}(n)=\left\lceil C(n^a+1)\right\rceil_+\qquad(C,a\in\mathbb R,\ n\in\mathbb N).$$

These interfaces connect the exact rational parameter certificate, finite local schedules, operational Light proofs, and the final deterministic integer 3SUM runtime statement. They retain the pinned source project's compiler and machine conventions.

/-!
# The compiler from the light language to the word RAM: cells, and the code of statements

This file holds the definitions: the cells, the code of expressions, tests, statements, calls and
returns, the length of each piece of code, and the one condition on the text of a program (its
width).  The code of a whole program, `compileProgram`, puts these pieces together.

**Cells.**  A memory cell a of the light language is the cell a ≥ 0 of the machine.  Everything else
lives in negative cells.  A whole program takes two arguments from the cells -1 and -2 (`cARG1`,
`cARG2`) and puts its result into the cell -3 (`cRESULT`); the cell -4 is not used.  Odd cells from
-5 down hold the registers of the compiled code, the temporaries T₀, T₁, … for the evaluation of
expressions, and a pool of numbers: the cell `cPool n` holds the number n, for all n up to the
largest position to return to.  Even cells hold the call stack: stack cell j is the cell -2 j
(`cStack`).  The outermost frame of a whole program begins at stack cell `mainFrame` = 4, so the
code of its statements writes no stack cell before the cell -8 and leaves the cells -1, …, -4
alone.  The lemmas about pieces of code ask less: only that a frame begins after stack cell 0.

**Numbers.**  The constants of the program text are built from their binary digits where they are
needed.  The numbers that the compiled code itself needs, offsets in a frame and positions to return
to, come from the pool: the length of the code that builds a number from its digits depends on the
number, and a position to return to depends on the lengths.

**Frames.**  With F local variables per procedure, the frame of a running procedure is given by a
number q: local variable x is the cell -2 (q + x), the position to return to is in the
cell -2 (q - 1), and the register FP holds -2 q.  A call moves q to q + F + 1.

**Jumps.**  The machine only has "branch if negative" to a fixed position.  An unconditional jump
tests a register that holds -1.  A return loads the position r to return to into the register RR and
jumps to the dispatcher, the code "RR := RR - 1; if RR < 0 go to j" for j = 0, 1, 2, …, which
arrives at position r after 2 (r + 1) steps: a constant for a fixed program.

**Calls.**  The caller evaluates the arguments into temporaries, computes the address of the new
frame, fills its local variables (arguments first, then zeros), stores the position to return to,
moves FP and jumps to the procedure.  The procedure ends with its return sequence: result into RET,
position into RR, FP back to the caller's frame, jump to the dispatcher.  Back in the caller, RET is
stored into the variable that receives the result.

**Lengths.**  A jump forward needs the length of code that is not yet written, so the lengths are
defined on the text (`Expr.size`, `Cond.size`, `Stmt.size`) and then shown to be the lengths of the
code (`length_compileExpr`, `length_compileCond`, `length_compileStmt`).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Light.Compiler
open _root_.Light.Compiler

The names of the registers are written in capitals, as in the comments on the code. -/

/-! ## The width of a text

The compiled code gives every frame the same number F of local variables.  That is enough if F is at
least the width of every body: a number that bounds the variables, the arguments of each call, and
the temporaries that each expression needs.  Then 2 F + 1 temporaries are enough too: up to F

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var x => x + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op _ a b => max a.vars b.vars
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.vars

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var _ => 1

  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.height

/-!
# Proof rules for the light language

Ends lim P d s σ T Q says: the statement s, started in σ, ends within T steps in a state that
satisfies Q.  There is one rule for each construct; a rule turns a goal about a statement into goals
about its parts, so a proof follows the text of the program from top to bottom.  Recursion needs no
rule: a statement about a recursive procedure is proved by induction (in Lean) on a measure, and the
rule for calls unfolds the body.

There are three rules for loops: with an invariant indexed by the number of the round and a cost for
each round (Ends.while), the same with one cost for all rounds (Ends.whileConst), and, for a loop
whose number of rounds depends on the data, with a quantity that every round decreases
(Ends.whileVariant).

The file also has the basic facts about runs (a run stays a run when procedures are appended to the
program), notation for writing programs, the simplification set
`light_norm`, and the standing assumptions `Std` about the limits.
-/

/-!
# A running time that is realized on the word RAM

The deductions between running-time claims are made for an arbitrary reading `M : DetTimeModel` of
"is solved by a deterministic algorithm in time T".  `RealizedWithin` is the link to programs: the
problem is solved on the word RAM, in its input layout, within `c T + c` steps.

/-- `RealizedWithin` for a problem of the form of `EndStatement.lean`, on the instances of all
sizes, 0 included: for every exponent `κ` some program solves all instances whose numbers are
bounded by `U = n^κ`, within `c max(T, 0) + c` steps. (A running time `T n U` says nothing at
`n = 0`.) -/
def Realized (Q : _root_.EndStatement.Problem) (T : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ κ : ℕ, ∃ (P : List _root_.EndStatement.Instr) (b : ℕ) (c : ℝ), 0 ≤ c ∧
    _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.Solves (_root_.ThreeSumApsp.WordRam.ofEnd Q) P b (fun x => x.U = x.n ^ κ) (fun x => c * max (T x.n x.U) 0 + c)

An item statement bounds the steps of a program by `C (n^a + 1)`, with real numbers `C` and `a`.
The end statement uses Lean's core library only.  It asks for a step bound `T` with natural values
that depends on the size alone, and it writes `T(n) = O(n^r)`, for a rational `r = p/q`, as
`T(n)^q ≤ K n^p`.  Here the first bound, rounded up, is shown to be a bound of the second kind
(`bigO_stepBound`), and a program that meets the first is shown to meet the second
(`SolvedInTime.endStatement`).  The program and the slope of the word size stay the same.

publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
The arithmetic interfaces describe coefficient bounds $|a_j|\le U$ (using zero outside a coefficient list), and local cover parameters at length $464h$ for $h\in\mathbb N$. The local threshold is the output count times $2^{2h}$; a deterministically selected prime $p$ has square between that positive threshold and sixteen times it, and determines the local bucket cap. The executable integer schedule for $m\in\mathbb N$ is

$$k(m)=2\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt[3]{m}\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor,\quad b(m)=20\left\lfloor\frac{203889696m}{20000000000k(m)}\right\rfloor,\quad s(m)=b(m)k(m),$$
$$d(m)=2^{\lfloor62656016s(m)/1000000000\rfloor}.$$

The divisions here are natural-number divisions, including their total zero-denominator convention. The even-microblock construction follows the pinned Apache-2.0 upstream formalization.

The Light language has finite expression and statement trees, integer local variables and memory, arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication, memory accesses, branches, loops, and procedure calls. An execution judgment $\operatorname{Exec}(\lambda,P,d,s,\sigma,\sigma',c)$ records an execution of statement $s$ in finite program $P$, at call depth $d$, from state $\sigma$ to state $\sigma'$ in exactly $c$ steps. Limits $\lambda$ bound word magnitudes, memory addresses, and call depth; expression and test costs count their primitive operations. Memory-preservation predicates say that two memories agree on a specified set of natural addresses, including complements of output regions and cells below a free pointer.

For the target word RAM, the bundle defines an exact number of non-verdict steps between configurations, code placement at an instruction offset, agreement outside a set of integer addresses, and which instructions write only inside a specified set. For any parameter type $A$, domain $D\subseteq A$, and functions $f,g:A\to\mathbb R$, the one-sided domination predicate is

$$\exists C\ge0\;\forall x\in D,\quad f(x)\le Cg(x).$$

It also defines absolute bounds on all entries of an integer list. These interfaces support memory framing, compositional step counts, and asymptotic cost estimates in the complete deterministic integer 3SUM runtime proof; the definitions themselves do not assert the final solver theorem.

/-!
# Regions of the memory, and the cells that a step leaves alone

A region is given by its first address `a` and its number `n` of cells.  `Inside a n b` says that
the cell `b` lies in it, `Outside a n b` that it does not, and `Apart a n a' n'` that two regions do
not meet.  `InOrder top [(a, n), (a', n'), …]` says that the listed regions lie one behind the other
and end at or below `top`.  All of these abbreviate linear inequalities.

`SameOn K μ μ'` says that the memory `μ'` agrees with `μ` on every cell that satisfies `K`.  It is
the one notion of "these cells are unchanged": a routine promises `SameOn K μ μ'` for the cells
`K` that it leaves alone.  (It is `Set.EqOn μ' μ {b | K b}`, stated with a predicate: the conditions
`K b` that occur are linear inequalities between addresses and are used as such.)  The usual choices
of `K` have names.

* `SameOutside μ μ' a n`: all cells outside one region; `SameOutside2` and `SameOutside3`: all cells
  outside two or three regions.
* `Kept μ μ' fr`: all cells below the free pointer `fr`.
* `KeptBut μ μ' fr out len`: all cells below `fr` outside the region of an output.

## How a fact is carried from one memory to a later one

A predicate `X` about a memory has one lemma of the name `X.keep` and of the form

  `theorem X.keep (h : X μ …) (hs : SameOn K μ μ' := by light_keep) : X μ' …`

where `K` describes the cells that `X` reads; `Seg.keep` is the model.  The argument `hs` has a
default proof.  So `h.keep`, with no argument, stands for "`h` still holds in the memory that is
asked for here".  The default proof `light_keep` uses every hypothesis of the form `SameOn _ ν ν'`
in the context, that is, the promises of the steps that were taken since `h` was obtained, and the
inequalities in the context that say where the regions lie.  In the proofs a promise is named when
the step is taken, as `same₂` in `rintro _ μ₂ ⟨sY, same₂⟩`.

`wrote μ dst f j` is the memory `μ` after a loop has written `f 0`, …, `f (j - 1)` to the cells from
`dst`.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Light
open _root_.Light


/-! ## Regions -/









/-! ## Memories that agree on some cells -/

/-- The memory `μ'` agrees with `μ` on every cell that satisfies `K`. -/
def SameOn (K : ℕ → Prop) (μ μ' : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop := ∀ b, K b → μ' b = μ b

/-- The memory `μ'` agrees with `μ` outside the `n` cells from address `a`. -/
abbrev SameOutside (μ μ' : ℕ → ℤ) (a n : ℕ) : Prop := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.SameOn (_root_.Light.Outside a n) μ μ'

/-- The memory `μ'` agrees with `μ` outside the `n` cells from `a` and the `m` cells from `b`. -/
abbrev SameOutside2 (μ μ' : ℕ → ℤ) (a n b m : ℕ) : Prop :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.SameOn (fun x => _root_.Light.Outside a n x ∧ _root_.Light.Outside b m x) μ μ'



/-- No cell below the free pointer has changed. -/
abbrev Kept (μ μ' : ℕ → ℤ) (fr : ℕ) : Prop := _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.SameOn (· < fr) μ μ'

/-- No cell below the free pointer has changed, except the `len` cells from `out`. -/
abbrev KeptBut (μ μ' : ℕ → ℤ) (fr out len : ℕ) : Prop :=
  _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.SameOn (fun x => x < fr ∧ _root_.Light.Outside out len x) μ μ'

/-!
# The light language

A small imperative language with procedures and recursion, in which the paper's procedures can be
written almost as printed.  It is a proof device: a program of this language is compiled
(`compileProgram`) to the word RAM of the end statement, and the compiler is proved to keep results
and, up to a constant factor that depends on the program text only, step counts.

* A program is a finite piece of data: a list of procedure bodies.  It contains no Lean functions.
* The memory is an array of integers addressed by natural numbers.  Each running procedure has local
  variables 0, 1, 2, ….
* Arithmetic: +, −, ×.  There is no division.  Comparisons (<, =) occur as the tests of if and
  while.
* Every executed operation costs one step: each constant, variable, operation and load of an
  expression, each comparison, assignment, store, branch, call and return.
* A run is subject to limits: it forms no value of absolute value above `word`, touches no cell at
  an address ≥ `space`, and nests calls at most `depth` deep.  A run that would break a limit does
  not exist.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Light
open _root_.Light






/-- Expressions: constants, local variables, operations, and the content of the memory cell at an
address. -/
inductive Expr : Type
  | const (n : ℕ)
  | var (x : ℕ)
  | op (o : _root_.Light.Op) (a b : Expr)
  | load (a : Expr)
  deriving Repr

/-- Tests. -/
inductive Cond : Type
  | lt (a b : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr)
  | eq (a b : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr)
  deriving Repr

/-- Statements.  `call p args x` runs procedure number p on the values of args and puts its result
into x. -/
inductive Stmt : Type
  | skip
  | set (x : ℕ) (e : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr)
  | store (a e : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr)
  | seq (s₁ s₂ : Stmt)
  | ite (c : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond) (s₁ s₂ : Stmt)
  | while (c : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond) (s : Stmt)
  | call (p : ℕ) (args : List _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr) (x : ℕ)
  deriving Repr

/-- A program: the bodies of its procedures, numbered from 0. -/
abbrev Program : Type := List _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt

/-- What a running procedure sees: its local variables and the memory. -/
structure State : Type where
  loc : ℕ → ℤ
  mem : ℕ → ℤ

/-- The limits on a run: largest absolute value of a word, number of memory cells, nesting depth of
calls. -/
structure Limits : Type where
  word : ℤ
  space : ℕ
  depth : ℕ

/-- The value of an expression. -/
def Expr.val (s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℤ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const n => n
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var x => s.loc x
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op o a b => o.eval (a.val s) (b.val s)
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => s.mem (a.val s).toNat

/-- The number of steps that evaluating an expression takes: one for each of its constants,
variables, operations, loads. -/
def Expr.cost : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const _ => 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var _ => 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op _ a b => a.cost + b.cost + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.cost + 1

/-- An address within the limits. -/
def Limits.Addr (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (a : ℤ) : Prop := 0 ≤ a ∧ a < lim.space

/-- The evaluation of an expression stays within the limits: every value that is formed fits in a
word, and every address that is read is within the memory. -/
def Expr.Safe (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr → Prop
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.const n => (n : ℤ) ≤ lim.word
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.var _ => True
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.op o a b => a.Safe lim s ∧ b.Safe lim s ∧ |o.eval (a.val s) (b.val s)| ≤ lim.word
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.load a => a.Safe lim s ∧ lim.Addr (a.val s)

/-- Whether a test holds. -/
def Cond.Holds (s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond → Prop
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => a.val s < b.val s
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => a.val s = b.val s

/-- The number of steps of a test: its two sides and the comparison. -/
def Cond.cost : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond → ℕ
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => a.cost + b.cost + 1
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => a.cost + b.cost + 1

/-- The evaluation of a test stays within the limits. -/
def Cond.Safe (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (s : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond → Prop
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.lt a b => a.Safe lim s ∧ b.Safe lim s
  | _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Cond.eq a b => a.Safe lim s ∧ b.Safe lim s





/-- `Exec lim P d s σ σ' c`: within the limits lim, and at nesting depth d of calls, the statement
s of the program P, started in the state σ, ends in the state σ' after exactly c steps. -/
inductive Exec (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (P : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Program) : ℕ → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State → ℕ → Prop
  | skip {d σ} : Exec lim P d _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.skip σ σ 0
  | set {d σ x e} : e.Safe lim σ →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.set x e) σ { σ with loc := Function.update σ.loc x (e.val σ) } (e.cost + 1)
  | store {d σ a e} : a.Safe lim σ → e.Safe lim σ → lim.Addr (a.val σ) →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.store a e) σ { σ with mem := Function.update σ.mem (a.val σ).toNat (e.val σ) }
        (a.cost + e.cost + 1)
  | seq {d σ σ' σ'' s₁ s₂ c₁ c₂} : Exec lim P d s₁ σ σ' c₁ → Exec lim P d s₂ σ' σ'' c₂ →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.seq s₁ s₂) σ σ'' (c₁ + c₂)
  | iteTrue {d σ σ' c s₁ s₂ k} : c.Safe lim σ → c.Holds σ → Exec lim P d s₁ σ σ' k →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s₁ s₂) σ σ' (c.cost + 1 + k)
  | iteFalse {d σ σ' c s₁ s₂ k} : c.Safe lim σ → ¬ c.Holds σ → Exec lim P d s₂ σ σ' k →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.ite c s₁ s₂) σ σ' (c.cost + 1 + k)
  | whileFalse {d σ c s} : c.Safe lim σ → ¬ c.Holds σ → Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.while c s) σ σ (c.cost + 1)
  | whileTrue {d σ σ' σ'' c s k₁ k₂} : c.Safe lim σ → c.Holds σ → Exec lim P d s σ σ' k₁ →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.while c s) σ' σ'' k₂ → Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.while c s) σ σ'' (c.cost + 1 + k₁ + k₂)
  | call {d σ σ' p args x body k} : (∀ e ∈ args, e.Safe lim σ) → P[p]? = some body → d < lim.depth →
      Exec lim P (d + 1) body ⟨_root_.Light.frame (args.map (·.val σ)), σ.mem⟩ σ' k →
      Exec lim P d (_root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Stmt.call p args x) σ ⟨Function.update σ.loc x (σ'.loc 0), σ'.mem⟩
        ((args.map _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Expr.cost).sum + 2 + k)

/-- Everything held in a variable or in a cell fits in a word. -/
def State.Bounded (lim : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.Limits) (σ : _root_.ThreeSum1960614.Machine.Light.State) : Prop :=
  (∀ x, |σ.loc x| ≤ lim.word) ∧ ∀ a, |σ.mem a| ≤ lim.word

end Light

end

/-!
# Running the word RAM: words, steps, pieces of code, straight-line code, branches

What the proofs about compiled code need to know about the word RAM in which the paper's claims are
stated.

* **Words.**  `wd W v` is the word of the integer v.  If v is in the range of signed words
  (`InRange`), the word gives back v (`toInt_wd`).
* **Steps.**  The end statement defines only whole runs (`exec`).  A configuration (`Cfg`) and a
  single step (`step`) are defined here; `exec_succ_of_step` and `exec_succ_of_verdict` say that
  `exec` takes one step at a time.
* **Runs.**  `Steps P n c c'`: exactly n steps lead from c to c', none of them a verdict.
  Runs are composed by `Steps.trans`; a run that ends before a verdict gives the value of `exec`
  (`exec_of_steps`), and more time does not change that value (`exec_mono`).
* **Code.**  `CodeAt P pos l`: the program P has the instructions of the list l from position pos
  on.
* **Straight-line code.**  Six instructions only change the memory (`Straight`, `effect`); a list
  of them runs through in its length (`steps_straight`).
* **Known numbers.**  On cells that hold the words of known numbers, an instruction writes the word
  of a known number: `effect_add`, …, `effect_store` for the memory; `steps_add`, `steps_sub`,
  `steps_load`, `steps_store` for the step.
* **Branches and verdicts.**  A branch on a cell that holds a known number is `steps_bltz`;
  `Steps.branch` turns its two outcomes into the two outcomes of a test.  The verdicts are
  `step_accept` and `step_reject`.
* **Framing.**  `AgreeOutside s m m'`: the memories m and m' are equal outside the set s of cells.
  For code without stores such a set can be read off the text (`WritesIn`, `agreeOutside_effects`).
-/

/-!
# Bounds up to a constant factor, in several parameters

The paper writes `f = O(g)` for functions of several parameters that are tied by side conditions,
such as `D ^ 18 ≤ n` for the parameters `n`, `D`, `w`. `Dominated dom f g` says this: there is a
constant `C ≥ 0` with `f x ≤ C * g x` for every tuple `x` of parameters that satisfies `dom x`. If
there is no side condition, `dom` is `fun _ => True`. The type `α` of the parameters is best a
structure with one named field for each of them, so that a bound reads
`Dominated (fun p => p.D ^ 18 ≤ p.n) (fun p => cost p) fun p => p.n ^ 2 / p.D`.

The lemmas of this file are the steps that the paper takes without comment: such bounds can be
chained (`Dominated.trans`), added (`Dominated.add`, `Dominated.add_add`), multiplied and divided
(`Dominated.mul`, `Dominated.mul_left`, `Dominated.const_mul`, `Dominated.pow`,
`Dominated.div_right`), joined by a case distinction (`Dominated.ite`), restricted to a smaller
domain (`Dominated.mono_dom`) and specialized (`Dominated.comp`). With them no proof has to name a
constant. A bound enters the calculus by `Dominated.of_le`, `Dominated.of_le_const_mul` or
`Dominated.of_exists_const`, and leaves it by `obtain ⟨C, hC, hle⟩` or `Dominated.exists_const_and`.
For functions of one natural number, `Dominated.of_eventually` takes a bound for all large `n`,
`Dominated.isBigO` gives Mathlib's `f =O[atTop] g`, and `isBigO_comp_add_one` substitutes a size
that need not tend to infinity.

In every closure lemma the bound comes first and the side conditions follow.

For nonnegative `f` and `g` the notion is Mathlib's `f =O[𝓟 {x | dom x}] g`, big-O along the
principal filter of the domain (`dominated_iff_isBigO_principal`). The one-sided form is taken
because a running time is bounded from above only.

## The notions of "bounded up to a constant" in this library

* `f =O[atTop] g` of Mathlib bounds `|f|` for large `n`. In this sense `IsBigOPow f a` is `O(n^a)`,
  `IsPowPolylog f a` is `O(n^a (log n)^e)` for some `e`, and `IsPowLittleO f a` is `n^{a+o(1)}`.
  The exponents of the theorems are stated with them.
* `UpperBigOPow`, `UpperPowPolylog` and `UpperPowLittleO` are the same three classes as bounds on
  `f` and not on `|f|`, for running times. A two-sided bound gives the one-sided one
  (`IsBigOPow.upperBigOPow`, `IsPowPolylog.upperPowPolylog`, `IsPowLittleO.upperPowLittleO`).
* `Dominated dom f g` bounds `f` on the whole domain, for several parameters. It comes from a bound
  for large `n` by `Dominated.of_eventually` and gives one by `Dominated.isBigO`.
* `Scale.SoftO t e` says that a count `t` with values in `ℕ` is `Dominated` by a monomial with the
  exponents `e`, up to powers of one more quantity; the tactic `growth` reads the exponents off an
  explicit expression. It gives a `Dominated` bound by `Scale.SoftO.dominated`. Its instance
  `SoftOSqrtPow` gives `IsPowPolylog` by `SoftOSqrtPow.isPowPolylog`.
-/

publish_jobs.theorem_title: Light-language execution and exact schedule foundations
publish_jobs.natural_language_statement:
The arithmetic interfaces describe coefficient bounds $|a_j|\le U$ (using zero outside a coefficient list), and local cover parameters at length $464h$ for $h\in\mathbb N$. The local threshold is the output count times $2^{2h}$; a deterministically selected prime $p$ has square between that positive threshold and sixteen times it, and determines the local bucket cap. The executable integer schedule for $m\in\mathbb N$ is

$$k(m)=2\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt[3]{m}\rfloor}{2}\right\rfloor,\quad b(m)=20\left\lfloor\frac{203889696m}{20000000000k(m)}\right\rfloor,\quad s(m)=b(m)k(m),$$
$$d(m)=2^{\lfloor62656016s(m)/1000000000\rfloor}.$$

The divisions here are natural-number divisions, including their total zero-denominator convention. The even-microblock construction follows the pinned Apache-2.0 upstream formalization.

The Light language has finite expression and statement trees, integer local variables and memory, arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication, memory accesses, branches, loops, and procedure calls. An execution judgment $\operatorname{Exec}(\lambda,P,d,s,\sigma,\sigma',c)$ records an execution of statement $s$ in finite program $P$, at call depth $d$, from state $\sigma$ to state $\sigma'$ in exactly $c$ steps. Limits $\lambda$ bound word magnitudes, memory addresses, and call depth; expression and test costs count their primitive operations. Memory-preservation predicates say that two memories agree on a specified set of natural addresses, including complements of output regions and cells below a free pointer.

For the target word RAM, the bundle defines an exact number of non-verdict steps between configurations, code placement at an instruction offset, agreement outside a set of integer addresses, and which instructions write only inside a specified set. For any parameter type $A$, domain $D\subseteq A$, and functions $f,g:A\to\mathbb R$, the one-sided domination predicate is

$$\exists C\ge0\;\forall x\in D,\quad f(x)\le Cg(x).$$

It also defines absolute bounds on all entries of an integer list. These interfaces support memory framing, compositional step counts, and asymptotic cost estimates in the complete deterministic integer 3SUM runtime proof; the definitions themselves do not assert the final solver theorem.
